questions.stem: What does an MSDS (also called an SDS) provide, and who mandates it?

choices.text: Handling and spill/fire information for hazardous materials, mandated by OSHA
Warranty terms for a device, mandated by the manufacturer
Network configuration details, mandated by the ISP
Software license terms, mandated by the vendor

questions.explanation: The Material Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is your handling and first-aid manual for hazardous items like toner and batteries - mandated by OSHA. It tells you what's in the product and how to handle a spill or fire.
questions.trap: MSDS is about hazardous-material safety, not warranties, networking, or software licensing.

questions.stem: How should used batteries and toner cartridges be disposed of?

choices.text: Recycled or taken to designated hazardous-waste facilities

questions.explanation: Batteries and toner cartridges must be recycled or disposed of at designated hazardous-waste facilities; many manufacturers include return labels.
questions.trap: These items cannot go in the regular trash - they are hazardous waste.

questions.stem: What is the target 'Goldilocks zone' for humidity in a server room, and why does it matter?

choices.text: Around 10%, to keep things very dry
Around 50%, balancing static risk (too low) against condensation/corrosion (too high)
Humidity has no effect on equipment

questions.explanation: Aim for about 50% humidity: too low risks static shock, too high risks condensation or corrosion.
questions.trap: Both extremes are harmful; 10% invites static and 90% invites corrosion. The balance point is ~50%.

questions.stem: A PC is clogged with dust. What is the recommended way to clean it?

choices.text: Use a standard vacuum inside the case
Blow it out with your breath
Take it outside and use compressed air

questions.explanation: Take a dusty PC outside and use compressed air. Keep the area ventilated.
questions.trap: Never use a standard vacuum inside a case - it generates static that can damage components.

questions.stem: Which power problems is a UPS specifically designed to keep systems running through?

choices.text: An outage, using a battery to keep systems running

questions.explanation: A UPS (uninterruptible power supply) uses a battery to keep systems running during an outage.
questions.trap: A UPS handles power issues (surges, sags, outages), not connectivity, cooling, or storage failures.

questions.stem: Which UPS type runs the device off the battery 100% of the time for zero switchover delay?
questions.explanation: An online UPS runs the load off the battery 100% of the time, giving zero transfer delay when utility power fails.
questions.trap: Standby switches over only when power fails (a brief delay); online has no delay because it's always on battery.

questions.stem: Which UPS type is described as fixing voltage drops (sags) without fully switching to battery?
questions.explanation: A line-interactive UPS corrects voltage drops (sags) on its own, between standby and online in capability.
questions.trap: Standby only kicks in on full power loss; the type that actively fixes voltage sags is line-interactive.

questions.stem: A site doesn't need battery backup but wants protection from voltage spikes. Which device fits?
questions.explanation: If you don't need battery backup, a surge suppressor still absorbs voltage spikes.
questions.trap: Any UPS includes a battery you don't need here; a surge suppressor handles spikes without that cost.

questions.stem: When buying a surge suppressor, what do you want from the joule rating and the let-through voltage?

choices.text: A high joule rating (over 600) and a low let-through voltage (ideally 330 V or less)
A low joule rating and a high let-through voltage
A joule rating of exactly zero and any let-through voltage
Joule and let-through ratings don't matter

questions.explanation: Look for a high joule rating (over 600 is best) and a low let-through voltage (ideally 330 V or less). Lower let-through means longer equipment life.
questions.trap: You want let-through LOW, not high - the lower the voltage that gets through, the better the protection.

questions.stem: On a surge suppressor, what does a lower let-through voltage rating mean for your equipment?
questions.explanation: Lower let-through leads to longer life - less excess voltage reaches the equipment.
questions.trap: Lower let-through is better, so it lengthens (not shortens) equipment life; it has nothing to do with internet speed.
